findings.diagnosis: The scorer routinely allows cuts that isolate sentence-final predicates/auxiliaries, negation, or closing punctuation as their own right-hand fragment — these positions nearly always flip or void the left fragment and should be treated as very bad cuts.
findings.evidence: ids: ["ja_jp_968","ja_jp_563","ja_jp_1584","ja_jp_1071","ja_jp_63","ja_jp_1187","ja_jp_1447","ja_jp_789","ja_jp_713","ja_jp_919"]; each policy kept a cut that leaves a trailing auxiliary/copula/negator or the closing mark as a separate segment (contra ≈ 1 and H near zero) and the offline target consistently removes that cut.

edit.text: If the right fragment begins with a sentence‑final auxiliary, copula, negation, or closing punctuation (i.e. material that completes or can flip the predicate), treat that cut as among the worst: rank it very low so it will not be chosen.

findings.diagnosis: The instruction to 'spread distinct integers across the full 0–100 range' pushes scorers to exaggerate separations and prevents clustering of many equally poor (or equally good) positions; this interacts badly with short‑latency bins and thins needed dense cuts.
findings.evidence: ids: ["ja_jp_1187","ja_jp_713","ja_jp_736","ja_jp_741","ja_jp_1447"]; these policies produce many tiny single‑character segments and preserve low‑quality cuts, while targets concentrate cuts into cohesive pieces—showing the current spreading rule harms dense, short‑chunk bins.

edit.target: Use the full 0-100 range to separate them; if two positions feel equal, decide which one you would rather cut at and score it higher.
edit.text: Do not require spreading scores across the entire 0–100 range. Use any distinct integers that preserve the ORDER by target; clustering adjacent ranks is allowed when targets are similar so short‑bin density is preserved.
